verdict: OK to lend in Tumakuru engineering & capital goods — pursue asset-backed component and machining SMEs feeding the new Tumakuru clusters; avoid pure EPC and thin-margin fabrication.
title: Tumakuru Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**An engineering unit in Tumakuru buys steel, castings and bought-out components, machines them, and sells to OEMs, railways, power T&D and data-centre supply chains.** Cash is made on the shop floor: machine hours, scrap control and order repeatability decide margin, not price lists. Value sits in the order book and the customer approval (vendor code), not in the fixed assets. **So when a proposal lands, check the customer concentration and whether the vendor code is approved and current; if one buyer is above half of sales, ask for the purchase order history and the approval letter.**

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is the whole game: receivables and inventory net of payables, and EPC-style execution stretches the cash conversion cycle well beyond OEM work [9][11].** Rating commentary notes payables have funded part of this cycle, which reverses the day a large customer slows payment [11]. Peer results show demand is real but margins are not automatic: Pitti is expanding through FY 2030 on data-centre, mining and railway orders while margins strain [4]; Suzlon grew revenue 26% to Rs 4,869 crore in Q2 FY27 but EBITDA stayed near Rs 720 crore and margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether volume growth is being bought with price; if EBITDA margin is below the prior year, ask for the customer-wise price revision.**

## The local growth opportunity
**Tumakuru itself is the story: gazette orders of 23 September 2026 cover 15 projects within 50 proposals envisaging Rs 2,152.13 crore of investment and about 8,944 jobs at CBIC TITL Vasanthanarasapura Phase-A [3].** Statewide, 27 new industrial parks are planned and roughly 1.25 lakh acres of KIADB land still needs fresh acquisition by 2047 [1]. Karnataka GST collections are up 11.1% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, and electricity demand up 23.3% against 9.5% [D]. **Pursue tier-2 machining, fabrication and component SMEs with a named OEM or park anchor as customer; avoid pure EPC bidders whose order book is unexecuted and whose bank guarantees are the real exposure [9].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle, not the order book: cash-flow-based limits, receivables-backed drawing power, and a bank guarantee sub-limit sized to live bids [9].** Take monthly stock and receivable statements, monthly bank statements, and quarterly GST returns reconciled to sales. **If receivables days cross the sanctioned cycle, cut drawing power immediately rather than renewing.** Peer DEE's Q3 FY26 revenue of Rs 286.7 crore and operating profit of Rs 47.6 crore show the upside when execution and piping demand align [5]; Skipper's record Q2 revenue and 56% PAT rise show export-led T&D strength [6]. **Prefer borrowers with export or T&D order visibility and a demonstrated payables cycle; avoid those funding capex from working capital.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the gap between sales growth and cash: if GST turnover rises while bank credits stay flat, the money is sitting in receivables.** Watch inventory days on raw steel, cheque returns, and any request to convert a BG limit into a fund limit. **If a borrower asks for a second bank for the same order, stop and re-check the order book.**
watch: Monthly bank statements and GST returns (monthly)
Credits flat while GST sales rise -> cut drawing power and ask for receivables ageing
Days exceed cycle by more than a fortnight -> freeze enhancement, seek customer confirmation of dues
Un-executed order book falls or BGs concentrate on one bid -> reduce non-fund limit
Margin falls with revenue growth -> ask for customer-wise price revision before renewal
Inventory days rise -> require stock statement and physical verification
